title: Shooting Stars and Meteorites
objective: After this level you can tell meteoroids, meteors and meteorites apart and explain meteor showers.
summary: A shooting star is a sand-grain meteoroid burning up. Meteor showers come from comet debris, like the August Perseids.

cards.headline: Most shooting stars are no bigger than a grain of sand.
Three names, one journey
cards.body: A meteoroid is a small piece of rock or debris in space. When it plunges into Earth’s atmosphere and burns up, the streak of light is a meteor, or shooting star. Any piece that survives to reach the ground is a meteorite.

cards.headline: Showers from comets
cards.body: Meteor showers happen when Earth passes through a trail of debris, usually dust a comet left behind (a few, like the Geminids, come from an asteroid). Most of those meteors come from particles about the size of a grain of sand, burning up as streaks of light.

cards.context: That’s when Earth crosses the debris of Comet Swift–Tuttle, one of the most reliable meteor showers of the year.

cards.headline: Shooting stars: explained
learned: Meteor: the streak of light in our sky
Meteorite: a piece that reaches the ground
Showers come from comet debris trails

questions.explanation: A comet leaves a trail of dust along its orbit. When Earth passes through it, many meteors streak across the sky.

questions.prompt: From Level 53: why does a comet leave a trail of dust that can later make meteors?

options.label: Near the Sun its ice turns to gas, releasing dust
Its tail breaks off every time it orbits
options.rationale: The dust comes from the ice vaporizing.

options.label: The solar wind grinds its rock into sand
options.rationale: The dust is freed as ice turns to gas.

options.label: It collides with asteroids on each orbit
options.rationale: The trail comes from the comet itself.

questions.explanation: As a comet nears the Sun, its ice turns to gas and releases dust, which spreads along its orbit.
